title: Checking Your Own Work
keyIdea: When you finish, look back before you say done. Count again, touching each thing once. Read your writing back. Ask: does my answer fit the question? Check a sum another way. Fix any slips, then say what you checked.

kid: When you finish, do not stop yet. Look back at your work. Ask: does this look right? Then you can say I am done.
Count again. Touch each thing one time. Pip wrote 4 apples, but there are 5. Pip fixed it.
Read your words back. Is there a capital at the start? A space between words? A full stop at the end?
Ask: does my answer fit the question? Try a sum a new way, with counters. Then say what you checked.
adult: This topic is self-checking. A child looks back over finished work without being asked, finds at least one error, and can say what they checked. It is an early step in metacognition: children learn to watch their own thinking instead of waiting for an adult to mark it.

The lab gives each kind of check its own action. Children recount apples, touching each one once. They read a sentence back and fix a capital letter, a finger space and a full stop. They decide if answers fit their questions, check sums with counters on a ten frame, and put the look-back steps in order.

Common mistakes: saying done as soon as the last mark is made; recounting by glancing instead of touching, so an item is skipped or counted twice; reading what they meant to write, not what is on the page; giving a true answer to a different question; and checking the same way twice, which repeats the same slip.
Build a short routine at home: finish, look back, fix, then say done. Ask what did you check? Praise the checking itself, most of all when your child finds their own slip.

familyTip: After a drawing, puzzle or bit of writing, ask "What will you check before you say done?" Let your child find one thing to fix by themselves, then ask them to tell you what they checked.

practice.prompt: Sam has just finished his work. What should he do first?
practice.hint: What comes between finish and done?
practice.explain: Look back first. Then fix any slips, and only then say done.

practice.prompt: Pip wrote {n} apples. Pip counts again and there are {=n+1}. What should Pip do?
practice.hint: Which number did the careful count find?
practice.explain: The careful count found {=n+1}, so Pip changes {n} to {=n+1}.

practice.prompt: Read it back: "the cat sat." What needs fixing?
choices: A capital T at the start
practice.explain: A sentence starts with a capital letter, so the needs a big T.

practice.prompt: Mia says {n} + 1 is {=n+2}. She checks with counters. What will she find?
choices: It is {=n+1}, so she fixes it
practice.hint: Put out {n} counters, then add one more. How many?
practice.explain: {n} counters and 1 more makes {=n+1}, not {=n+2}. Checking another way found the slip.

pool.hint: How did Pip count the apples?
pool.explain: Touching each thing once means you skip none and count none twice.

pool.prompt: "How many legs has a dog?" Leo says, "A dog has a tail." Does it answer the question?
choices: No, it is about a tail, not legs
pool.hint: What did the question ask about?
pool.explain: It is true, but the question was about legs. A dog has 4 legs.

pool.prompt: Read it back: "Iwent home." What is the slip?
choices: I and went need a space
pool.hint: Are the words too close together?
pool.explain: I and went are two words, so they need a finger space between them.

choices: Finish, look back, fix, say done
pool.hint: Think of the lab. Which step comes last of all?
pool.explain: You finish, look back, fix any slips, and say done last of all.

pool.prompt: Zak says {n} + 2 is {=n+3}. How can he check?
pool.hint: How did Pip check sums in the lab?
pool.explain: Counters show {n} and 2 more is {=n+2}, so Zak can fix {=n+3}.

pool.prompt: Ava counts {n} ducks, touching each one once. She wrote {n}. What now?
choices: It matches, so she can say done
Change it to a bigger number
pool.hint: Does her count match what she wrote?
pool.explain: Her careful count and her answer are both {n}, so the check says it is right.

pool.prompt: Gran asks, "What did you check?" What is a good answer?
choices: I read each line back for full stops
pool.hint: Can you say the check you did?
pool.explain: Saying what you checked, like reading back for full stops, shows you really looked.

pool.prompt: Sam checks his sum the same way twice and gets the same slip. What helps?
choices: Check another way, like with counters
pool.hint: What did the ten frame do in the lab?
pool.explain: A new way, like counters, can show a slip that the first way keeps missing.

visual.caption: Is it a way to check your work? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: recount Pip's apples one touch each, read a sentence back to fix it, test if answers fit, check sums with counters and order the look-back steps.
